Neonatal Salmon sharks (Lamna ditropis) emerge from their mothers at a relatively large size, a trait common among lamnid sharks that invest heavily in individual offspring. At birth, the precaudal length typically measures 62.5 centimeters [Lb = 62.5 centimeters], with a reported range of 60 to 65 centimeters (60-65 centimeters) [Lb = 60-65 centimeters] in the published literature. This size at parturition is substantial compared to many other elasmobranchs, reflecting a lengthy gestation period that is presumed to occur at an elevated uterine temperature of 15.7 °C [T = 15.7 °C], which is derived from an assumed ambient environmental temperature of 4.7 °C plus an increment of 11 °C during incubation. The corresponding wet weight at birth is approximately 5.42 kilograms [Wwb = approximately 5.42 kilograms], a mass that places the neonatal shark in a favorable position to begin foraging on small pelagic fishes and squids immediately after parturition. The gestation period, from fertilization to birth, has been estimated to last about 274.5 days [ab = about 274.5 days], a notably long developmental phase for a cold-water shark.

As Salmon sharks grow, they undergo a prolonged juvenile and sub-adult phase before reaching the large body sizes that characterize the species. Female individuals ultimately achieve a significantly greater maximum precaudal length than their male counterparts, reaching 217 centimeters [Li = 217 centimeters]. Males, in contrast, attain a smaller ultimate precaudal length of 190 centimeters [Li = 190 centimeters]. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in maximum size is consistent with the reproductive strategy of many lamniform sharks, where larger females can accommodate a greater litter size or larger pups. The asymptotic masses associated with these lengths are substantial, with females reaching a maximum wet weight of 238.4 kilograms [Wwi = 238.4 kilograms] and males attaining 159.2 kilograms [Wwi = 159.2 kilograms]. These values represent the largest recorded adult body sizes for the species and are derived from length-weight regressions established for the North Pacific population.

The onset of puberty in Salmon sharks occurs at a size well below the ultimate maximum, distinguishing the sub-adult stage from the reproductively active adult period. Females achieve sexual maturity at a precaudal length of 175 centimeters [Lp = 175 centimeters], corresponding to a fork length that typically falls within the range of 165 to 180 centimeters. The wet weight at puberty for females is estimated at 124 kilograms [Wwp = 124 kilograms]. Males, following the pattern observed in maximum size, mature at a smaller precaudal length of 140 centimeters [Lp = 140 centimeters], with a corresponding wet weight at puberty of 62.9 kilograms [Wwp = 62.9 kilograms]. The attainment of these sizes marks the transition from the immature organism to a reproductively viable elasmobranch, a shift that is associated with gonad maturation and the onset of testicular recrudescence in males. Field studies indicate that the age at which these pubertal sizes are reached is influenced by food availability and environmental temperature.

Once mature, the maximum reproductive rate of Salmon sharks is constrained by the species' low fecundity and biennial breeding cycle. Females typically produce a single litter of 4 pups [N_R_i = single litter of 4 pups] every two years [F_R_i =  every two years], a pattern that results in a low annual reproductive output relative to many other fish species. This reproductive strategy is thought to be an adaptation to the cold, productive waters of the North Pacific, where the ambient environmental temperature averages approximately 4.7 °C [T = 4.7 °C], and the sharks themselves are active at a temperature of 9.7 °C [T = 9.7 °C] during their metabolic and foraging periods. The extended interval between litters allows females to rebuild substantial energy reserves, which are stored as lipids in the large liver characteristic of lamnid sharks. A gravid female shark may invest a considerable proportion of her body mass into the developing embryos, which rely on oophagy throughout gestation.

The lifespan of the Salmon shark is consistent with its slow life-history pace, characterized by late maturity, low fecundity, and a long reproductive tenure. Maximum longevity has been estimated at approximately 27 years [am = approximately 27 years] under the thermal conditions experienced by the species in its natural environment, corresponding to an ambient environmental temperature of 4.7 °C [T = 4.7 °C]. This extended lifespan allows for multiple reproductive events over the course of an individual's life, despite the long interval between successive litters. Compared to other large pelagic sharks such as the shortfin mako (Isurus oxyrinchus), the Salmon shark exhibits a similar or slightly greater maximum age, which aligns with its cold-water habitat and relatively slow metabolic rate. The species eventually undergoes natural mortality through senescence or age-related physiological deterioration, completing a life cycle that is finely tuned to the seasonal rhythms and prey availability of the subarctic North Pacific Ocean.
